chunks: Muhammad wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him): A man has a hundred dirhams due from another man, so he presses him for it, and he says to him, 'I will come to you in ten days and pay your need, and if I do not come, then a thousand dirhams are due from me, payable immediately without any condition, and I will have it witnessed upon me.' Then he called them to witness, and he (peace be upon him) signed: 'It is not fitting for them to testify except with the truth, nor is it fitting for the creditor to take anything except the right (original amount), God willing.'

key_terms.دِرْهَم: Dirham, a silver coin used as currency

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on taking a larger penalty amount when a debtor fails to pay on time?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the distinction between a conditional penalty and a genuine debt, ruling that the creditor is entitled only to the principal amount (one hundred dirhams) rather than the inflated thousand, as the larger sum serves merely as a guarantee. This ruling underscores the Shia legal principle of fairness in financial transactions, ensuring that witness testimony and subsequent claims reflect the actual obligation rather than a punitive clause. It highlights the Imam’s emphasis on 'al-haqq' (the right/truth) in commercial dealings, preventing exploitation through ambiguous contractual terms.
